Beginning with <s>Maghā</s>, one should go south; beginning with <s>Anurādhā</s>, west.
A northern journey is praised among the seven beginning with <s>Dhaniṣṭhā</s>.
<s>Aśvinī</s>, <s>Revatī</s>, <s>Citrā</s>, and <s>Dhaniṣṭhā</s> are auspiciously adorned.
<s>Mṛgaśiras</s>, <s>Aśvinī</s>, <s>Citrā</s>, <s>Puṣya</s>, <s>Mūla</s>, and <s>Hasta</s> are always auspicious
for giving a maiden in marriage, for journeys, for consecrations, and for similar rites.

children.text: śukracandrau hi janmasthau śubhadau ca dvitīyake
children.translated_text: Venus and the Moon, when in the natal sign and in the second, bestow good fortune.
The Moon, Mercury, Venus, and Jupiter are auspicious in each sign, and then in the third.
Mars, Saturn, the Moon, the Sun, and Mercury are best in the fourth.
Venus and Jupiter are best in the fifth, and the Moon and <s>Ketu</s> when properly joined.

children.text: mandākārai ca kujaḥ ṣaṣṭhe gurucandrau ca saptame
children.translated_text: Saturn, the Sun, and Mars are auspicious in the sixth; Jupiter and the Moon in the seventh.
Mercury and Venus are best in the eighth; Jupiter situated in the ninth is auspicious.
The Sun, Saturn, and the Moon are auspicious in the tenth; all planets are auspicious in the eleventh.

children.text: budho 'tha dvādaśe caiva bhārgavaḥ sukhado bhavet ||
children.translated_text: And in the twelfth, Mercury and <s>Bhārgava</s>, Venus, are givers of happiness.

children.text: siṃhena makaraḥ śreṣṭhaḥ kanyayā meṣa uttamaḥ
children.translated_text: With <s>Siṃha</s>, <s>Makara</s> is best; with <s>Kanyā</s>, <s>Meṣa</s> is excellent.
With <s>Tulā</s> there is <s>Mīna</s>, and with <s>Kumbha</s> there is <s>Karkaṭa</s>.

children.text: dhanuṣā vṛṣabhaḥ śreṣṭho mithunena ca vṛścikaḥ
children.translated_text: With <s>Dhanuṣ</s>, <s>Vṛṣabha</s> is best; and with <s>Mithuna</s>, <s>Vṛścika</s>.
These six-eight relationships indeed produce affection; there is no doubt.

children.text: iti śrīgāruḍe mahāpurāṇe pūrvakhaṇḍe prathamāṃśākhye ācārakāṇḍe jyotiḥśāstre grahāṇāṃ śubhāśubhasthānādinirūpaṇaṃ nāmaikaṣaṣṭitamo 'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the glorious <s>Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa</s>, in the eastern section called the first part, in the ācāra division, the sixty-first chapter, called "The Description of the Auspicious and Inauspicious Positions of the Planets and Related Matters" in the science of jyotiṣa.
<s>Hari</s> said:
I shall briefly describe the marks of men and women; listen, O <s>Śaṅkara</s>.
Feet that do not sweat, whose soles are soft and resemble the inside of a lotus,
with joined toes, copper-colored nails, fine ankles, and no visible veins,

children.text: kūrmonnatau ca caraṇau syātāṃ nṛpavarasya hi ||
children.translated_text: and raised like a tortoise, are the feet of the best of kings.
Nails that are rough and pale, feet that are crooked and marked by raised veins,
The feet, shaped like winnowing baskets, dry, and with sparse toes,
would give suffering and poverty; no deliberation is needed here.
Shanks furnished with little hair and shaped like an elephant's trunk are excellent.
Among great-souled kings there is one hair in each pore.

children.text: dve dve romṇī paṇḍitānāṃ śrotriyāṇāṃ tathaiva ca ||
children.translated_text: Among learned men and likewise among <s>śrotriyas</s> (Vedic scholars), there are two hairs in each pore.
Three hairs belong to poor men; one whose knees are fleshless is diseased.
A man with a small <s>liṅga</s> (male organ) is wealthy, but without sons and the like.
One with a thick <s>liṅga</s> is poor; one with a single testicle is unhappy.

children.text: viṣame strīcañcalo vai nṛpaḥ syādvṛṣaṇe same ||
children.translated_text: When the testicles are uneven he is fickle with women; when the testicles are even, he becomes a king.
One with hanging testicles is short-lived, without wealth, and has a defective <s>maṇi</s> (glans).
With pale and also darkened <s>maṇis</s> (glans-marks), a man is happy.
The poor have noisy urination; kings have a silent stream.
Those whose bellies are even are rich in enjoyments; those whose bellies resemble pots are poor.
Those with snake-like bellies are poor; lifespan is declared by means of lines.

children.text: lalāṭe yasya dṛśyante tisro rekhāḥ samāhitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: If three regular lines are seen on a man's forehead,

children.text: sukhī putrasamāyuktaḥ sa ṣaṣṭiṃ jīvate naraḥ
children.translated_text: that happy man, endowed with sons, lives sixty years.
From the sight of two lines a man lives forty years.
With one line he lives twenty years; lines extending to the ears give a lifespan of one hundred years.
A pair of lines gives seventy years of life, while with three lines the lifespan becomes sixty.
With lines partly distinct and partly indistinct, a man has a lifespan of twenty years.
A man with deficient lines lives forty years.
And with broken lines there is surely untimely death for a man.

children.text: triśūlaṃ paṭṭiśaṃ vāpi lalāṭe yasya dṛśyate
children.translated_text: If a trident or a <s>paṭṭiśa</s> (spear) is seen on a man's forehead,
endowed with wealth and sons, he lives a hundred autumns.
The life-line is in the middle between the index finger and the middle finger;

children.text: samprāptā yā bhavedrudra sa jīveccharadaḥ śatam ||
children.translated_text: when it reaches there, O <s>Rudra</s>, he lives a hundred autumns.
The first is the knowledge-line, which follows from the thumb.
The line going to the base of the middle finger is thereafter the life-line.
The life-line may enter, taking support on the little finger.

children.text: acchinnā vā vibhaktā vā sa jīveccharadaḥ śatam ||
children.translated_text: Whether unbroken or divided, he lives a hundred autumns.
The line in whose palm reveals that person's lifespan;

children.text: śatavarṣāṇi jīvecca bhogī rudra na saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: he lives a hundred years and is an enjoyer, O <s>Rudra</s>; there is no doubt.
Taking support on the little finger and reaching the middle finger,
the life-line makes a human being have a lifespan of sixty years.

children.text: iti śrīgāruḍe mahāpurāṇe pūrvakhaṇḍe prathamāṃśākhye ācārakāṇḍe jyotiḥśāstre sāmudrike puṃllakṣaṇanirūpaṇaṃ nāma triṣaṣṭitamo 'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, called 'Description of the Marks of Men,' in the <s>Sāmudrika</s> section of the <s>Jyotiḥśāstra</s> within the <s>Ācārakāṇḍa</s>, named the first part of the <s>Pūrvakhaṇḍa</s>, in the blessed great <s>Garuḍapurāṇa</s>.
<s>Hari</s> said:

children.text: yasyāstu kuñcitāḥ keśā mukhaṃ ca parimaṇḍalam
children.translated_text: The maiden whose hair is curled and whose face is round,
and whose navel turns to the right, increases her family.
And she who has the luster of gold and red lotus-like hands,
among thousands of women, she too becomes devoted to her husband.

children.text: vakrakeśā ca yā kanyā maṇḍalākṣī ca yā bhavet
children.translated_text: The maiden whose hair is crooked and who has round eyes,

children.text: bhartā ca mriyate tasyā niyataṃ duḥkhabhāginī ||
children.translated_text: her husband surely dies, and she becomes a sharer in sorrow.
The maiden with a face like the full moon and radiance like the young sun,

children.text: viśālanetrā bimboṣṭhī sā kanyā labhate sukham ||
children.translated_text: wide-eyed and with bimba-fruit lips, obtains happiness.
With many lines there is distress; with few, lack of wealth.
With red lines she obtains happiness; with black lines she goes to servitude.

children.text: kārye ca mantrī satstrī syātsatī syātkaraṇeṣu ca
children.translated_text: In affairs a good wife should be a counselor; in actions she should be faithful.

children.text: streheṣu bhāryā mātā syādveśyā ca śayane śubhā ||
children.translated_text: In affections the wife should be a mother, and in bed she is auspicious as a courtesan.

children.text: aṅkuśaṃ kuṇḍalaṃ cakraṃ yasyāḥ pāṇitale bhavet
children.translated_text: If a goad, an earring, or a discus is present in a woman's palm,

children.text: putraṃ prasūyate nārī narendraṃ labhate patim ||
children.translated_text: that woman gives birth to a son and obtains a king as husband.

children.text: yasyāstu romaśau pārśvau romaśau ca payodharau
children.translated_text: If a woman's sides are hairy and her breasts are hairy,

children.text: unnatau cādharoṣṭhau ca kṣipraṃ mārayate patim ||
children.translated_text: and her lower lips are prominent, she quickly brings about her husband's death.
If in a woman's palm there is a line like a rampart and gateway,
even if born in a family of slaves, she attains queenship.
If her line of hair is raised, tawny, and continuous,
even if born in a royal family, she attains slavery.
If a woman's ring toes and big toes do not stand upon the ground,
she quickly brings about her husband's death and acts according to her own will.
If by the mere act of her walking a trembling of the ground arises,
she quickly brings about her husband's death and acts according to her own will.
From the glossiness of the eyes comes good fortune; from the glossiness of the teeth, food.

children.text: tvacaḥ snehena śayyāṃ ca pādasnehena vāhanam ||
children.translated_text: From the glossiness of the skin comes a bed, and from the glossiness of the feet, a vehicle.
A woman's feet are auspicious when they are smooth, raised, and have coppery nails,
marked with signs of fish, goad, and lotus, and marked with discus and plough.
Not sweating and soft-soled, a woman's feet are praised.

children.text: śubhe jaṅghe virome ca ūrū hastikaropamau ||
children.translated_text: Her shanks are auspicious when hairless, and her thighs when like an elephant's trunk.
A broad secret part resembling an aśvattha leaf is excellent.
A praised navel is deep, right-turning, and auspicious.
A woman should be hairless, with three folds; her chest and breasts should be devoid of hair.

children.text: iti śrīgāruḍe mahāpurāṇe pūrvakhaṇḍe prathamāṃśākhye ācārakāṇḍe jyotiḥśāstre sāmudrike strīlakṣaṇanirūpaṇaṃ nāma catuḥṣaṣṭitamo 'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, called 'Description of the Marks of Women,' in the <s>Sāmudrika</s> section of the <s>Jyotiḥśāstra</s> within the <s>Ācārakāṇḍa</s>, named the first part of the <s>Pūrvakhaṇḍa</s>, in the blessed great <s>Garuḍapurāṇa</s>.
<s>Hari</s> said:
I shall declare the auspicious marks of men and women, as spoken by <s>Samudra</s>,
by the mere knowledge of which there is certainty about past and future.
Not sweating, soft-soled, and resembling the interior of a lotus,
The feet are auspicious when the toes are close together, the nails copper-colored, and the feet free from prominent veins and projections.
For a king they are remembered as raised like a tortoise, with hidden ankles and good heels.

children.text: śūrpākārau virūkṣau ca vakrau pādau śirālakau ||
children.translated_text: Feet shaped like winnowing baskets, rough, crooked, and full of veins,
dried up, with pale nails, belonging to a destitute man, and with sparse toes,
feet rough with the thorns of the road and likewise astringent-colored,
bring severance of the lineage; when resembling spikes, they mark a slayer of a Brahmin.
Sparse-haired shanks indicate one who delights in going to forbidden women.
Soft-haired, even shanks, with the appearance of an elephant's trunk,
and well-developed thighs in proper proportion to the knees are remembered as belonging to a king.
A destitute man has jackal-like shanks and one hair in each pore.

children.text: nṛpāṇāṃ śrotriyāṇāṃ ca dve dve śriye ca dhīmatām ||
children.translated_text: For kings and learned Brahmins, and for intelligent men, two hairs in each pore indicate prosperity.
With three or more hairs, men are destitute, ill-natured, and censured.

children.text: keśāśca vai kuñcitāśca pravāse mriyate naraḥ ||
children.translated_text: And if the hairs are curled, a man dies away from home.
A fleshless knee indicates good fortune; small and depressed knees indicate attachment to women.

children.text: vikaṭaiśca daridrāḥ syuḥ samāṃsai rājyameva ca ||
children.translated_text: With misshapen knees people become poor; with evenly fleshed knees, kingship indeed is indicated.
Large organs are said to indicate long life; a man with a small penis is wealthy.
One with a thick penis is childless and devoid of wealth.
If the penis is dwarfish, he will be without sons and wealth.
If it is crooked, he may otherwise have sons; if it bends downward, poverty results.

children.text: alpe tvatanayo liṅge śirāle 'tha sukhī naraḥ
children.translated_text: With a small penis he is without offspring; if it is veined, the man is happy.
When the penis has large knots, he is endowed with sons and the like.
With the scrotum hidden, and with long, bent parts, he is deprived of wealth.
That same man, if he emits lightly, is strong and warlike.
With one testicle he is weak; with uneven testicles he is fickle among women.
With even testicles he is said to be a king; with pendulous ones he lives a hundred years.
With raised testicles he is long-lived, and with rough glanses he is a lord.
With pale glanses men are destitute; with soiled ones they enjoy happiness.
Men whose urination is noisy or noiseless become poor.
With one, two, three, four, five, or six streams,
and with urine moving in a clockwise turn, they are remembered as kings.
Those with scattered urine are destitute, while principal streams give happiness.
Women are indicated by a single stream and by smooth, raised glanses.
With even ones, men are rich in women, jewels, and wealth; with those depressed in the middle, daughters are indicated.
With dry ones they are poor, and with shrivelled ones they are proclaimed unfortunate.

children.text: puṣpagandhe nṛpāḥ śukre madhugandhe dhanaṃ bahuḥ ||
children.translated_text: If the semen smells of flowers, men are kings; if it smells of honey, there is much wealth.

children.text: putrāḥ śukre matsyagandhe tanuśukre ca kanyakāḥ
children.translated_text: If the semen smells of fish, there are sons; if the semen is scanty, daughters.
If it smells of meat, he is a great enjoyer; if it smells of rutting ichor, he will be a sacrificer.
If it smells alkaline, he is poor; one quick in intercourse is long-lived.
One not quick in intercourse is short-lived; one with large buttocks is devoid of wealth.

children.text: māṃsalasphik sukhī syācca siṃhasphik bhūpatiḥ smṛtaḥ
children.translated_text: With fleshy buttocks he is happy, and with lion-like buttocks he is remembered as a king.
With a lion-like waist he becomes a king; a man with a monkey-like waist is destitute.

children.text: sarpodarā daridrāḥ syuḥ piṭharaiśca ghaṭaiḥ samaiḥ
children.translated_text: Those with snake-like bellies are poor; those with bellies like bowls and jars,
and with broad sides, are wealthy; with red, sunken sides, they are destitute.
With even armpits they are rich in enjoyment; with sunken armpits, devoid of wealth.
Those with raised armpits are kings; those with crooked, uneven armpits are bad.
Men with fish-like bellies are very wealthy; by their navels they are remembered as happy.
With wide, large, depressed navels they partake of suffering.
A navel situated in the middle of folds causes pain like colic.
A left-turning navel gives success, and a right-turning one gives intelligence.
One extended to the side gives long life, while one set inward makes a lord of wealth.
One pointing downward makes a man rich in cattle, and a lotus-pericarp shape gives kingship.
One belly-fold gives a hundred-year life; two folds are remembered as bringing prosperity and enjoyment.
Three folds indicate a lord of the earth or a teacher; with straight folds, one is happy.
A crooked belly-fold marks one who approaches forbidden women; kings have fleshy sides
with soft, very even hairs turning clockwise.
With the opposite marks they are servants of others, without property, and deprived of happiness.
With nipples that are not raised, men become fortunate.
With uneven and long nipples they are poor; with yellowish and well-developed ones, kings.
A heart or chest that is evenly raised, unmoving, fleshy, and broad
belongs to kings; for low men it is rough-haired and full of veins.
One with an even chest is wealthy; with full chest-parts he is strong.
With uneven chest-parts he is poor; such men also meet death by a weapon.
With uneven collarbones men are poor, and likewise with bones that seem bound together.
With raised collarbones they enjoy pleasures; with depressed ones they are destitute; with full ones they are endowed with wealth.
A flat-necked man is poor; one whose throat is veined and dry is happy.
One with a buffalo-like neck is brave; one with a deer-like neck is struck down by a weapon.
With a conch-like neck he is a king; with a long neck, an excessive eater.
A hairless, bent back is auspicious; otherwise it is inauspicious.
Armpits like leaves of the aśvattha are best, fragrant, and with deer-like hair.
Otherwise they are a cause of poverty and lack of wealth.

children.text: saṃmāsau caiva bhugnālpau śliṣṭau ca vipulau śubhau ||
children.translated_text: The two shoulders, slightly bent, close-set, and broad, are auspicious.

children.text: ā jānulambitau bāhū vṛttau pīnau nṛpeśvare
children.translated_text: Arms reaching to the knees, round and full, belong to a lord of kings.
For the destitute they are hairy and short; they are excellent when they have the appearance of an elephant's trunk.
The fingers of the hands are auspicious when furnished with openings for air.

children.text: medhāvināṃ ca sūkṣmāḥ syurbhṛtyānāṃ cipiṭāḥ smṛtāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Fine fingers belong to the intelligent, while flattened ones are remembered as belonging to servants.
People with thick fingers are poor; likewise, those with bent and very thin fingers are so.
Those whose hands are like a monkey's are poor, while strength belongs to those whose hands are like a tiger's.
Men whose palms are sunken suffer the destruction of their paternal wealth.
With wrists that are hidden, well joined, and fragrant,
men become kings; with deficient nails and noisy joints they are bereft of wealth.
Those with covered and depressed marks are proclaimed wealthy.
Those whose hands are stretched open are givers; men with uneven hands are themselves uneven in character.
With hands and palms red like lac, men become lords.

children.text: paradāraratāḥ pītai rūkṣair niḥsvā narā matāḥ
children.translated_text: Those with yellow palms delight in others' wives; men with rough palms are considered poor.
Those whose nails are like husks are impotent; men with crooked and cracked nails
are poor when their nails are bad, and, likewise, those with discolored nails are contentious with others.
With copper-colored nails men become kings, and with thumbs marked like barley-corns they are wealthy.
Marks arising at the base of the thumb indicate sons; one whose finger-joints are long
is long-lived and fortunate, while one with sparse fingers is poor.
One with close-set fingers is wealthy; and if someone has three lines
on the palm, rising up from the wrist, he has the sign of a king.
A man marked with a pair of fish becomes a giver of charitable feasts.
Thunderbolt-shaped marks belong to the wealthy, as do marks resembling a fish-tail, O wise one.
Marks like a conch, parasol, palanquin, elephant, or lotus belong to a king.
Marks like a pot, elephant-goad, banner, or lotus-fiber belong to a lord of treasures.
Marks like garlands belong to those rich in cattle; a svastika-like mark belongs to a great king.
Marks like a discus, sword, javelin, bow, or lance are found in a king's hand.
A mortar-like mark belongs to one rich in sacrifices, and an altar-like mark to an agnihotrin.
Marks like a reservoir or sacred water-channel, and triangular marks, belong to a righteous man.
Lines at the base of the thumb signify sons, and fine ones signify daughters.
A line going along the index finger and reaching the base of the little finger

children.text: śatāyuṣaṃ ca kurute chinnayā taruto bhayam
children.translated_text: makes a man live a hundred years; if it is broken, there is danger from a tree.
Those with many lines are poor, and those with thin chins are without property.
With fleshy chins men possess wealth; with reddish lower lips they become kings.
With lips like the bimba fruit there is auspiciousness, but with split, rough, broken,
and uneven lips men are without wealth. Teeth that are glossy and close-set are auspicious.

children.text: tīkṣṇā dantāḥ samāḥ śreṣṭhā jihvā raktā samā śubhā ||
children.translated_text: Sharp and even teeth are best; a red and even tongue is auspicious.

children.text: ślakṣṇā dīrghā ca vijñeyā tālū śvete dhanakṣaye
children.translated_text: It should be known as smooth and long; if the palate is white, there is loss of wealth.

children.text: kṛṣṇe ca paruṣo vakraṃ samaṃ saumyaṃ ca saṃvṛtam ||
children.translated_text: If it is black, the person is harsh; the mouth should be straight, even, gentle, and closed.
For kings it is spotless and smooth; the opposite belongs to the miserable.
Great suffering belongs to the unlucky; one with a woman-like face obtains a son.

children.text: āḍhyānāṃ vartulaṃ vakraṃ nirdravyāṇāṃ ca dīrghakam
children.translated_text: The wealthy have a round mouth, while the propertyless have a long one.
A fearful or crooked mouth marks an evil-doer, and a square one belongs to rogues.
A sunken mouth belongs to the sonless, and a short one to the miserly.

children.text: sampūrṇaṃ bhogināṃ kāntaṃ śmaśru snigdhaṃ śubhaṃ mṛdu ||
children.translated_text: A full and lovely one belongs to enjoyers; a glossy, auspicious, soft beard
is compact and has unsplit tips, while a red beard marks a thief.
Those with red, scanty, and rough beards and ears meet an evil death.
With fleshless and flattened ears men lack enjoyments; the miserly have short ears.
Conch-shaped ears belong to kings, while hairy ears belong to those whose life is spent.
Those with large ears are proclaimed wealthy and royal.
Kings have ears that are glossy, well attached, hanging, and fleshy.
One with sunken cheeks is an enjoyer, while a minister has full cheeks.
One with a parrot-like nose is happy, and one with a dry nose lives very long.
One whose nose has a cut tip and a hollow is attached to intercourse with forbidden women.
With a long nose there is good fortune, while a thief has a contracted organ.
Death comes to one with a flattened nose; he is inferior among the fortunate.

children.text: svalpacchidrau supuṭau ca avakrau ca nṛpeśvare ||
children.translated_text: Small nostrils, good nasal cavities, and an unbent nose belong to a lord of men.

children.text: krūre dakṣiṇavakrā syād balināṃ ca kṣutaṃ sakṛt
children.translated_text: A nose bent to the right belongs to the cruel; among the strong, a single sneeze

children.text: syād viniṣpiṇḍitaṃ hrādi sānunādaṃ ca jīvakṛt ||
children.translated_text: that is compact, pleasant, and resonant is life-giving.
Those with eyes whose ends are curved and which resemble lotus petals share in happiness.
One with cat-like eyes is sinful; those with honey-brown eyes are wicked-hearted.
The squint-eyed are cruel, and green-eyed men are tainted.
Men with crooked eyes are brave, and elephant-eyed men are commanders of armies.
Those with deep eyes become lords, and those with large eyes become ministers.
Blue-lotus-eyed men are learned, and good fortune belongs to those with dark eyes.
For those whose eyes have black pupils, there is said to be the tearing out of the eyes.
Round-eyed men are sinful, and men with wretched eyes are poor.
A glossy and broad gaze brings enjoyment; one that is too high-set brings short life.
Broad and raised brows bring happiness, while uneven brows bring poverty.
One with dense, long, joined brows, and with fine brows raised like the young moon,

children.text: āḍhyo niḥsvaśca khaṇḍabhrūr madhye ca vinatabhruvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: is wealthy; but one with broken brows, or brows bent in the middle, is poor.

children.text: strīṣu gamyāsu saktāḥ syuḥ sutārthe parivarjitāḥ
children.translated_text: Such men are attached to women who may be approached and are deprived in the matter of sons.
With raised and broad temples and with uneven foreheads,
men are poor; with foreheads resembling a half-moon they are wealthy.
Teachers have broad, shell-like foreheads; those with visible veins are evil-doers.
With grain-like marks, with veins, and with svastika marks, men become lords of wealth.
Those with sunken foreheads deserve bondage and likewise delight in cruel deeds.
With contracted foreheads men are miserly, while with raised foreheads they become kings.
Weeping without tears, smooth and not wretched, gives good fortune to men.

children.text: pracurāśrudīnaṃ rūkṣaṃ ca ruditaṃ ca sukhāvaham
children.translated_text: Weeping that is full of tears, piteous, and harsh also brings happiness.
Laughter without trembling is best; laughter with closed eyes brings misfortune.
Repeated laughter is bad, for it is connected in many ways with madness.
Three lines extending across the forehead belong to those who live a hundred years.
With four lines there will be kingship, and then the lifespan is ninety-five years.
With no line the lifespan is ninety years; with broken lines men are licentious.
With lines reaching the edge of the hair, a man will have a lifespan of eighty years.
With five, seven, or six lines, and likewise with many, the lifespan is fifty years.
With crooked lines it is forty years; with lines going down to meet the eyebrows it is thirty.
With lines curving to the left the lifespan is twenty; with small lines it is short.
Those whose heads are umbrella-shaped are kings; one with a sunken head is wealthy.
With flattened heads there is the death of the father; with round heads there are cattle and other possessions.
A pot-headed man has evil tastes and is deprived of wealth and the like.
With black, curled hair, glossy, each hair growing singly,
with tips unbroken, soft, and not excessively numerous, men become kings.
With many-rooted, uneven hair, thick at the tips and tawny,
and with very curly, dense, black hair, men are poor.
Whatever limb is very rough, veined, and lacking flesh,
all of that is inauspicious; otherwise it is the opposite.
He is broad in three places, deep in three, long in five, and fine in five.
Raised in six places, short in four, and red in seven, that man is a king.

children.text: nābhiḥ svaraśca sasattvaṃ ca trayaṃ gambhīramīritam ||
children.translated_text: The navel, the voice, and inner vigor are declared to be the three deep things.
For a man, the forehead, face, and chest should be very broad.

children.text: cakṣuḥ kakṣā nāsikā ca ṣaṭ syur nṛpakṛkāṭikāḥ ||
children.translated_text: The eyes, armpits, nose, and nape are the six royal points.

children.text: unnatāni ca hrasvāni jaṅghā grīvā ca liṅgakam
children.translated_text: The shanks, neck, and penis are raised and short.
The back is the fourth; the red parts are the palms, soles, lower lip, and nails,
the corners of the eyes, the feet, the tongue, and the lips; five things are fine.
The teeth, finger-joints, nails, hair, and skin are auspicious when fine.
Long are the space between the breasts, the arms, the teeth, the eyes, and the nose.

children.text: narāṇāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ proktaṃ vadāmi strīṣu lakṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: The marks of men have been stated; now I shall tell the marks among women.

children.text: rājñyāḥ snigdhau samau pādau talau tāmrau nakhau tathā
children.translated_text: A queen has smooth and even feet, and copper-colored soles and nails.
Her toes are close-set and raised at the tips; by obtaining her, a man becomes a king.
Her ankles are concealed and well-formed, and her soles, beautiful like lotuses, are auspicious.
They do not sweat, their soles are soft, and they are marked with fish, goad, and banner.
They have marks of thunderbolt, lotus, and plough; a slave-woman's feet are otherwise.

children.text: jaṅghe ca romarahite suvṛtte visire śubhe ||
children.translated_text: Shanks that are hairless, well-rounded, and without visible veins are auspicious.
A joint-region that is not prominent and a pair of even knees are auspicious.

children.text: ūrū karikarākārāv aromau ca samau śubhau ||
children.translated_text: Thighs shaped like elephant trunks, hairless and even, are auspicious.
A broad private part resembling an aśvattha leaf is excellent.
For women, the front of the hips and a thigh raised like a tortoise are auspicious.

children.text: gūḍho maṇiśca śubhado nitambaśca guruḥ śubhaḥ
children.translated_text: A hidden jewel is good-giving, and heavy buttocks are auspicious.
Broad, fleshy, deep, and wide is auspicious.
The navel should turn clockwise, and the waist should be adorned with three folds.
Breasts that are hairless, full, firm, and not uneven are auspicious.

children.text: kaṭhinau romaśā śastā mṛdugrīvā ca kambubhā
children.translated_text: They should be hard; a soft neck shaped like a conch is praised.
Reddish lips are best, and the face should be fleshy and round.
The teeth should be like jasmine flowers, and the speech like that of a cuckoo.
Speech joined with graciousness, free of deceit, is pleasing like the call of a haṃsa.

children.text: nāsā samā samapuṭā strīṇāṃ tu rucirā śubhā
children.translated_text: For women, an even nose with equal nostrils is beautiful and auspicious.
The eye should be like a blue lotus, not joined to the nose and not drooping.

children.text: na pṛthū bālendunibhe bhruvau cātha lalāṭakam
children.translated_text: The brows should not be broad, but like the young moon; and then the forehead
is auspicious when shaped like a half-moon, not high, and without hair.
The pair of ears should be well-fleshed, even, soft, and well-set.

children.text: snigdhā nīlāśca mṛdavo mūrdhajāḥ kuñcitāḥ kacāḥ ||
children.translated_text: The hair of the head should be glossy, blue-black, soft, and the locks curled.

children.text: strīṇāṃ samaṃ śiraḥ śreṣṭhaṃ pāde pāṇitale 'thavā
children.translated_text: For women an even head is best; on the foot or on the palm,
with marks of horse, elephant, <s>Śrī</s>, tree, sacrificial post, arrow, barley, and lance,
with banners, chowries, garlands, mountains, earrings, and altars,
with conches, umbrellas, lotuses, fish, svastikas, and fine chariots,
and with marks such as the goad, women become beloved of kings.
The wrists should be concealed, and the hands like lotus buds.

children.text: na nimnaṃ nonnataṃ strīṇāṃ bhavetkaratalaṃ śubham
children.translated_text: For women, an auspicious palm should be neither sunken nor raised.
When furnished with lines, it makes a woman non-widowed and one who enjoys conjugal pleasure.

children.text: rekhā yā maṇibandhotthā gatā madhyāṅguliṃ kare ||
children.translated_text: The line in the hand that arises from the wrist and goes to the middle finger,

children.text: gatā pāṇitale yā ca yordhvapādatale sthitā
children.translated_text: and the one that extends in the palm or is set upward in the sole of the foot,

children.text: strīṇāṃ puṃsāṃ tathā sā syādrājyāya ca sukhāya ca ||
children.translated_text: for women and for men alike, is for sovereignty and happiness.
A line arising from the base of the little finger makes a person live a hundred years.
When it is situated in the space between the forefinger and the middle finger,
if it is deficient it causes a deficient lifespan; so too do lines going to the base of the thumb.
Large lines are said to indicate sons, while thin ones indicate daughters.
Much-broken lines indicate short life; long unbroken lines indicate long life.

children.text: śubhaṃ tu lakṣaṇaṃ strīṇāṃ proktaṃ tvaśubhamanyathā ||
children.translated_text: The auspicious marks of women have been stated; the inauspicious are the opposite.

children.text: kaniṣṭhikānāmikā vā yasyā na spṛśate mahīm
children.translated_text: If a woman's little toe or ring toe does not touch the ground,

children.text: aṅguṣṭhaṃ vā gatātītya tarjanī kulaṭā ca sā ||
children.translated_text: or if the second toe passes beyond the big toe, she is unchaste.
Above the two calves, if the shanks are very veined...
and when there is hairiness and excessive fleshiness, and likewise a pot-shaped belly,
the private part of unhappy women is left-turning, sunken, and small.

children.text: grīvayā hrasvayā niḥsvā dīrghayā ca kulakṣayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: With a short neck a woman is poor, and with a long one there is destruction of the family.
With a broad neck women become fierce; of this there is no doubt.

children.text: kekare piṅgale netre śyāme lolekṣaṇā satī ||
children.translated_text: If the eyes are squinting and tawny, and a dark woman has restless eyes,

children.text: smite kūpe gaṇḍayośca sā dhruvaṃ vyabhicāriṇī
children.translated_text: and if, when she smiles, there are hollows in her cheeks, she is certainly adulterous.

children.text: pralambinī lalāṭe tu devaraṃ hanti cāṅganā ||
children.translated_text: A woman with an overhanging forehead kills her husband's younger brother.

children.text: udare śvaśuraṃ hanti patiṃ hanti sphicordvayoḥ
children.translated_text: A mark on the belly kills the father-in-law; on the two buttocks it kills the husband.

children.text: yā tu romottarauṣṭhī syānna śubhā bhartureva hi ||
children.translated_text: A woman whose upper lip has hair is certainly not auspicious for her husband.

children.text: stanau saromāv aśubhau karṇau ca viṣamau tathā
children.translated_text: Breasts with hair are inauspicious, and so too ears that are uneven.

children.text: karālā viṣamā dantāḥ kleśāya ca bhavanti te ||
children.translated_text: Terrible and uneven teeth become a cause of suffering.
Black gums lead to theft, and long teeth to the death of the husband.
With hands having the forms of flesh-eating beasts, resembling wolves, crows, and the like,
veiny, uneven, and dry, women indeed become devoid of wealth.
A woman whose upper lip is raised is quarrelsome and speaks harshly.
These are faults among misshapen women; thereafter the leaf-shaped form is among the virtues.
The marks of men and women have been stated; I shall now tell that which gives knowledge of them.

children.text: iti śrīgāruḍe mahāpurāṇe pūrvakhaṇḍe prathamāṃśākhye ācārakāṇḍe jyotiḥśāstre sāmudrike strīnaralakṣaṇaṃ nāma pañcaṣaṣṭitamo 'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the glorious <s>Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa</s>, in the eastern section called the first part, in the ācāra division, the sixty-fifth chapter, called "The Marks of Women and Men" in the science of jyotiṣa and sāmudrika.
<s>Hari</s> said:
Even one without marks becomes auspicious through the worship of a stone marked with a discus.
First is the <s>Sudarśana</s> form; then the supreme <s>Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa</s>.
With three discs it is <s>Acyuta</s>; with four discs it is <s>Caturbhuja</s>.
Then <s>Vāsudeva</s> and <s>Pradyumna</s>, and after that <s>Saṅkarṣaṇa</s>, are remembered.
The eighth is <s>Puruṣottama</s>; the ninth is <s>Navavyūha</s>, and the tenth is <s>Daśātmaka</s>.
The eleventh is <s>Aniruddha</s>, and the twelfth is <s>Dvādaśātmaka</s>.
Beyond that it is <s>Ananta</s>, according to the lines and other marks on the disc, in order.
Stones marked as <s>Sudarśana</s>, when worshipped, grant every desire.
Where there is a <s>śālagrāma</s> stone and the deity born in <s>Dvāravatī</s>,

children.text: ubhayoḥ saṃgamo yatra tatra muktirna saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: where there is the union of the two, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt.

children.text: śālagrāmo dvārakā ca naimiṣaṃ puṣkaraṃ gayā
children.translated_text: <s>Śālagrāma</s>, <s>Dvārakā</s>, <s>Naimiṣa</s>, <s>Puṣkara</s>, and <s>Gayā</s>,
<s>Vārāṇasī</s>, <s>Prayāga</s>, <s>Kurukṣetra</s>, and <s>Sūkara</s>,

children.text: gaṅgā ca narmadā caiva candrabhāgā sarasvatī
children.translated_text: the <s>Gaṅgā</s> and <s>Narmadā</s>, and also <s>Candrabhāgā</s> and <s>Sarasvatī</s>,
<s>Puruṣottama</s> and <s>Mahākāla</s>: these are the sacred places, O <s>Śaṅkara</s>.
They remove all sins and indeed bestow enjoyment and liberation.
<s>Prabhava</s>, <s>Vibhava</s>, <s>Śukla</s>, <s>Pramoda</s>, and then <s>Prajāpati</s>,

children.text: aṅgirāḥ śrīmukho bhāvaḥ yuvā dhātā tathaiva ca
children.translated_text: <s>Aṅgiras</s>, <s>Śrīmukha</s>, <s>Bhāva</s>, <s>Yuvan</s>, and likewise <s>Dhātṛ</s>,
<s>Īśvara</s>, <s>Bahudhānya</s>, <s>Pramāthin</s>, <s>Vikrama</s>, and <s>Viṣu</s>,
<s>Citrabhānu</s>, <s>Svarbhānu</s>, <s>Tāraṇa</s>, <s>Pārthiva</s>, and <s>Vyaya</s>,
<s>Sarvajit</s>, <s>Sarvadhārin</s>, <s>Virodhin</s>, <s>Vikṛti</s>, and <s>Khara</s>,
<s>Nandana</s> and <s>Vijaya</s>, and also <s>Jaya</s>, <s>Manmatha</s>, and <s>Durmukha</s>,
<s>Hemalamba</s>, <s>Vilamba</s>, <s>Vikāra</s>, <s>Śarvarī</s>, and <s>Plava</s>,
<s>Śubhakṛt</s>, <s>Śobhana</s>, <s>Krodhin</s>, <s>Viśvāvasu</s>, and <s>Parābhava</s>,
<s>Plavaṅga</s>, <s>Kīlaka</s>, <s>Saumya</s>, <s>Sādhāraṇa</s>, and <s>Virodhakṛt</s>,

children.text: paridhāvī pramādī ca ānando rākṣaso nalaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Paridhāvin</s>, <s>Pramādin</s>, <s>Ānanda</s>, <s>Rākṣasa</s>, and <s>Nala</s>,
<s>Piṅgala</s>, <s>Kāla</s>, <s>Siddhārtha</s>, <s>Raudra</s>, and likewise <s>Durmati</s>,
<s>Dundubhi</s>, <s>Rudhirodgārin</s>, <s>Raktākṣa</s>, <s>Krodhana</s>, and <s>Akṣaya</s>.
These years are inauspicious or auspicious by their very names.
I shall describe time, for the sake of success, O <s>Rudra</s>, through the rise of the five vowels.

children.text: rājā sājā udāsā ca pīḍā mṛtyustathaiva ca ||
children.translated_text: There are <s>Rājā</s>, <s>Sājā</s>, <s>Udāsā</s>, <s>Pīḍā</s>, and likewise <s>Mṛtyu</s>.

children.text: ā ī ū ai au svarāṃśca likhetpañcāgnikoṣṭhake
children.translated_text: One should write the vowels ā, ī, ū, ai, and au in a five-fire grid.
The lines go vertically and horizontally, arranged according to the sequence of the six fires.
The lunar days are placed in the single-fire squares; three are <s>Rājā</s>, then those of <s>Sājā</s>.
<s>Udāsā</s>, <s>Mṛtyu</s>, and <s>Pīḍā</s> follow, and <s>Kuja</s> and the son of <s>Soma</s> in order,
then <s>Guru</s> and <s>Śukra</s>, <s>Manda</s>, and the Sun and Moon, as stated.
The nakṣatras beginning with <s>Revatī</s> and ending with <s>Mṛgaśiras</s> are the first kalā.
Elsewhere the asterisms are in groups of five each, and the rising is likewise from <s>Caitra</s> onward.
At intervals of twelve days, the first syllable of the names of two months is likewise used.

children.text: kalāliṅgā ca yā tiṣṭhetpañcamastasya vai mṛtiḥ
children.translated_text: Whatever kalā-mark is present there, the fifth from it is indeed that person's death.

children.text: kalā tithistathā vāro nakṣatraṃ māsameva ca ||
children.translated_text: The kalā, lunar day, weekday, nakṣatra, and month,

children.text: nāmodayasya pūrvaṃ ca tathā bhavati nānyathā
children.translated_text: and before them the rising of the name: so it comes to pass, and not otherwise.
Oṃ kṣaiṃ, homage to <s>Śiva</s>.
The formula beginning with kṣāma, the limbs of <s>Śiva</s>, the gaze, removes poison, seizure by spirits, and hostile intent.
The seed-syllable of <s>Nṛsiṃha</s>, placed in a lotus, bewilders the three worlds.
<s>Mṛtyuñjaya</s>, <s>Gaṇa</s>, and <s>Lakṣmī</s>, when written with rocanā and the other substances,

children.text: bhūrje tu dhāritāḥ kaṇṭhe bāhau ceti jayādidāḥ ||
children.translated_text: and worn on birch bark at the throat or on the arm, grant victory and the like.

children.text: iti śrīgāruḍe mahāpurāṇe pūrvakhaṇḍe prathamāṃśākhye ācārakāṇḍe jyotiḥśāstre śālagrāmaṣaṣṭyūbdasvarodayānāṃ nirūpaṇaṃ nāma ṣaṭṣaṣṭitamo 'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the glorious <s>Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa</s>, in the eastern section called the first part, in the ācāra division, the sixty-sixth chapter, called "The Explanation of Śālagrāmas, the Sixty Years, and the Rise of the Vowels" in the science of jyotiṣa.
<s>Sūta</s> said:

children.text: hareḥ śrutvā haro gaurīṃ dehasthaṃ jñānamabravīt ||
children.translated_text: After <s>Hara</s> heard from <s>Hari</s>, he spoke to <s>Gaurī</s> the knowledge situated in the body.

children.text: kujo vahnī raviḥ pṛthvī saurirāpaḥ prakīrtitaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Kuja</s> is fire, the Sun is earth, and <s>Sauri</s> is declared to be water.
<s>Rāhu</s>, situated in the region of wind, illuminates the right aperture.
<s>Guru</s>, <s>Śukra</s>, <s>Saumya</s>, and the Moon are the fourth group.
One should make the left nāḍī stand in the middle for oneself.
When the moving breath is joined with <s>Iḍā</s>, then one should perform actions:
attendance at one's post, meditation, trade, and an audience with the king.
One should carefully cause other auspicious acts to be done.
But when the right channel is flowing, <s>Śani</s>, <s>Bhauma</s>, and <s>Saihika</s> are active.
And <s>Ina</s> as well; likewise there is the rise of the malefics.
For the discrimination of auspicious and inauspicious is known from the rise of the breath.
Within the body are channels, manifold and very extensive.
Below the navel is the bulb; from there shoots go forth.
Seventy-two thousand are established in the middle of the navel.
They stand like a wheel, and all are remembered as bearers of the vital breath.
Among them three are best: the left, the right, and the middle.
The left is said to have the nature of the moon, and the right is like the sun.
The middle is fire; producing its result, it completes the time.
The left, being of the form of nectar, is established in refreshing the world.
The right, with a fierce aspect, always dries up the world.
When both flow, there is death, destructive of every undertaking.

children.text: nirgame tu bhavedvāmā praveśe dakṣiṇā smṛtā
children.translated_text: At exhalation the left is to be understood; at inhalation the right is remembered.
In the course of <s>iḍā</s> there is gentleness; likewise it has the movement of moon and sun.
One should perform fierce actions when the breath is established in <s>piṅgalā</s>.
For travel, for all undertakings, and for removing poison, <s>iḍā</s> is prescribed.
In eating, sexual union, and battle, <s>piṅgalā</s> bestows success.
In rites such as expulsion and killing, among these acts <s>piṅgalā</s> is prescribed.
In sexual union, in combat, and in eating it bestows success.
For auspicious undertakings, for travel, and for acts concerning poison,
<s>iḍā</s> should be employed by kings for peace, liberation, and attainment of aims.
When the flow is through both, fierce and gentle acts should be avoided.
The wise man should know it to be like poison and should recollect it carefully.
In gentle and auspicious acts, in gain, victory, and life,
and in going and coming, the left is honored everywhere.

children.text: yuddhādibhojane ghāte strīṇāṃ caiva tu saṃgame ||
children.translated_text: In battle and the like, in eating, in striking, and in union with women,
the right channel is praised; at entry it is used for petty or lower rites.
Auspicious and inauspicious actions, gain and loss, victory and defeat,
and life or non-life: whatever one asks about, the middle does not succeed.
Whether in the left course or in the right, where the questioner has confidence,

children.text: tanusthaḥ pṛcchate yastu tatra siddhirna saṃśayaḥ
children.translated_text: if he asks while it is present in the body, there success occurs, without doubt.
When the free-flowing one, <s>Vāmadeva</s>, flows within oneself,
if one asks while standing in that part, success becomes fruitless.

children.text: vāme vā dakṣiṇe vāpi yatra saṃkramate śivā ||
children.translated_text: On the left or on the right, wherever the auspicious one passes over,

children.text: ghore ghorāṇi kāryāṇi saumye vai madhyamāni ca
children.translated_text: in a fierce condition one should do fierce acts, and in a gentle one, moderate acts.

children.text: prasthite bhāgato haṃse dvābhyāṃ vai sarvavāhinī ||
children.translated_text: When the <s>haṃsa</s> has set out by its portion, flowing through both channels,
then the yogin skilled in yoga should recognize death.
Wherever he stands and asks, facing left or right,
there and there one should always indicate the rising of the wind equally.

children.text: agrato vāmikā śreṣṭhā pṛṣṭhato dakṣiṇā śubhā ||
children.translated_text: In front, the left channel is best; behind, the right is auspicious.

children.text: vāmena vāmikā proktā dakṣiṇe dakṣiṇā śubhā
children.translated_text: On the left the left channel is declared auspicious; on the right the right is auspicious.

children.text: vāme vāmā śubhe caiva dakṣiṇe dakṣiṇā śubhā ||
children.translated_text: On the left the left is auspicious, and on the right the right is auspicious.

children.text: jīvo jīvati jīvena yacchūnyaṃ tastvaro bhavet
children.translated_text: The living one lives by the living breath; when it is empty, the breath is absent.
Whatever undertaking has been specified, marked by victory and other auspicious signs,
all of that certainly comes about in the full channel.
Up to the boundary of the other channel, three fortnights are taught.

children.text: yāvatṣaṣṭhī tu pṛcchāyāṃ pūrṇāyāṃ prathamo jayet
children.translated_text: Up to the sixth day, in a question, when the channel is full, the first party wins.
But when it is empty, one should say without hesitation that the second party wins.
A wind corresponding to the left course arises, granting success in action.
When the right path has begun, if there is an uneven path, the syllable is uneven.

children.text: anyatra vāmavāhe tu nāma vai viṣamākṣaram
children.translated_text: Elsewhere, when the left is flowing, the name has an uneven number of syllables.
Then that warrior obtains victory in the midst of battle.
But when the right wind is flowing, if the name has an even number of syllables,

children.text: jāyate nātra sandeho nāḍīmadhye tu lakṣayet ||
children.translated_text: it comes to pass; there is no doubt. One should observe it within the channel.
When the breath has entered <s>piṅgalā</s>, one conquers the pacifying battle.
As long as the movement lasts up to the rise of the channel, one should reach that direction.

children.text: na dātuṃ jāyate so 'pi nātra kāryā vicāraṇā
children.translated_text: He is not able to give it; no deliberation should be made about this matter.

children.text: atha saṃgrāmamadhye tu yatra nāḍī sadā vahet ||
children.translated_text: Now, in the midst of battle, wherever the channel is always flowing,

children.text: sā diśā jayamāpnoti śūnye bhaṅgaṃ vinirdiśet
children.translated_text: that direction obtains victory; in the empty direction one should declare defeat.
When the course is born, one should know victory; when it is dead, one should declare death.

children.text: jayaṃ parājayaṃ caiva yo jānāti sa paṇḍitaḥ
children.translated_text: He who knows victory and defeat is learned.

children.text: vāme vā dakṣiṇe vāpi yatra saṃcarate śivam ||
children.translated_text: On the left or on the right, wherever the auspicious current moves,
having set out on that path, one obtains it; the journey is continually favorable.
When the moon-flow or sun-flow is present, one should engage in battle.

children.text: yastu pṛcchati tatrasthaḥ sa sādhur jayati dhruvam
children.translated_text: The good man who asks while standing there surely wins.

children.text: yāṃ diśaṃ vahate vāyustāṃ diśaṃ yāvadājayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In whatever direction the wind flows, up to that direction there is victory.
There is no doubt; if the hostile one is standing in front,

children.text: meṣyādyā daśa yā nāḍyo dakṣiṇā vāmasaṃsthitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: the ten channels beginning with <s>Meṣī</s>, situated on the right and the left,

children.text: care sthire tadvimārge tādṛśe tādṛśe kramāt
children.translated_text: move in the movable and fixed signs, and on the contrary path, each in its own order.

children.text: nirgame nirgamaṃ yāti saṃgrahe saṃgrahaṃ viduḥ ||
children.translated_text: At going out, it goes out; at gathering in, they know it as gathering in.
Having heard the questioner's words, one should discern it by the bell-shaped form.

children.text: vāme vā dakṣiṇe vāpi pañcatattvasthitaḥ śive ||
children.translated_text: On the left or on the right, when the auspicious one is established in the five elements,
fire is above, water below, and wind is situated crosswise.

children.text: madhye tu pṛthivī jñeyā nabhaḥ sarvatra sarvadā ||
children.translated_text: Earth is to be known in the middle, and ether is everywhere, always.
Above is death; below is peace; crosswise the wise man should expel.
In the middle one should recognize the pillar; liberation is everywhere, all-pervading.

children.text: iti śrīgāruḍe mahāpurāṇe pūrvakhaṇḍe prathamāṃśākhye ācārakāṇḍe svarodaye śubhāśubhanirūpaṇaṃ nāma saptaṣaṣṭitamo 'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, called 'Determination of the Auspicious and Inauspicious in Svarodaya,' in the section on conduct, in the first part called the Pūrvakhaṇḍa, in the venerable great <s>Garuḍapurāṇa</s>.
<s>Sūta</s> said:
I shall describe the examination of jewels. There was an asura named <s>Bala</s>.
<s>Indra</s> and the others were conquered by him, and he could not be defeated by them.
Under the pretext of a boon, the gods asked him to become a sacrificial victim at a sacrifice.

children.text: balo dadau sa paśutām atisattvasurair hataḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Bala</s> granted that victimhood, and he was slain by the gods, who were of very great strength.
He was cut up by them like a sacrificial animal, bound by the thunderbolt of his own word.
<s>Bala</s> did this for the sake of the worlds, desiring the welfare of the gods.
Because his essential being was pure, and because of his pure act,
all the limbs of his body became seeds of jewels.
Then, for the gods, the <s>Yakṣas</s>, the <s>Siddhas</s>, and the wind-consuming beings,
there arose at that time a very great taking up of the jewel-seed itself.
As they were falling swiftly through the sky in an aerial vehicle,
whatever seed of jewels fell anywhere at all,

children.text: mahodadhau sariti vā pavarta kānane 'pi vā
children.translated_text: whether in the great ocean, in a river, on a mountain, or even in a forest,
that place became a mine, according to the importance of the site and the deposit.
Among them appear jewels that destroy rākṣasas, poison, snakes, and disease, and remove sin,
and likewise jewels that are defective.
Diamond, pearls, together with rubies and emeralds, are mentioned,
and also excellent blue sapphires, vaidūrya gems, and yellow topazes.
Karketana, pulaka, the gem called rudhira, and also crystal,
as well as coral-gem, have been carefully specified in summary by those who know them.

children.text: ākāravarṇau prathamaṃ guṇadoṣau tatphalaṃ parīkṣā ca
children.translated_text: Form and color first, then qualities and defects, their effect, and the examination,
and also the value, should be understood by experts in jewels from all the treatises.
Those that arise under bad ascendants and on an afflicted day
are also joined with faults and are diminished in the wealth of their qualities.
A ruler of the earth who desires prosperity should wear
or collect jewels that have been purified by examination.
Those who know the śāstra and are skilled, the examiners who possess jewels,
are proclaimed to be the knowers of the measure of value.
Since diamond is declared by the wise to have great power,
this examination begins with diamond; therefore it is now set forth by us.

children.text: tasyāsthileśo nipapāta yeṣu bhuvaḥ pradeśeṣu kathaṃcideva
children.translated_text: In whatever regions of the earth a small piece of his bone somehow fell,
there diamonds of many shapes arise from him who wished to conquer the thunderbolt-weapon.
<s>Haima</s>, <s>Mātaṅga</s>, <s>Saurāṣṭra</s>, <s>Pauṇḍra</s>, <s>Kaliṅga</s>, <s>Kosala</s>,
<s>Veṇvātaṭa</s>, together with <s>Sauvīra</s>, are the eight producing regions of diamond.

children.text: ātāmrā himaśailajāśca śaśibhā veṇvātaṭīyāḥ smṛtāḥ sauvīre tvasitābjameghasadṛśās tāmrāśca saurāṣṭrajāḥ
children.translated_text: Those born from the snowy mountains are slightly coppery; those from <s>Veṇvātaṭa</s> are remembered as moon-bright; in <s>Sauvīra</s> they are like dark lotuses and clouds, and those born in <s>Saurāṣṭra</s> are coppery.

children.text: kāliṅgāḥ kanakāvadātarucirāḥ pītaprabhāḥ kosale śyāmāḥ puṇḍrabhavā mataṅgaviṣaye nātyantapītaprabhāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Those from <s>Kaliṅga</s> are lovely with a gold-white luster; in <s>Kosala</s> they have a yellow radiance; those born in <s>Pauṇḍra</s> are dark; in the <s>Mātaṅga</s> region they have a not excessively yellow brilliance.

children.text: atyarthaṃ laghu varṇataśca guṇavatpārśveṣu samyak samaṃ rekhābindukalaṅkakākapadakatrāsādibhir varjitam
children.translated_text: If any diamond seen anywhere in this world, even one as small as an atom, is extremely light, excellent in color, perfectly even on its sides, and free from lines, dots, stains, crow's-foot marks, cracks, and the like,

children.text: loke 'smin paramāṇumātram api yadvajraṃ kvacid dṛśyate tasmindevasamāśrayo hyavitathastīkṣṇāgradhāraṃ yadi ||
children.translated_text: then, if it has a sharp-tipped edge, the abode of the gods in it is unfailing.
Among diamonds, the embodied forms of the gods are also said to be determined by arrangement of color;
and the classification should be made from the colors, precisely on the basis of color.
Green, white, yellow, tawny, dark, and copper-red, naturally beautiful,
are the respective colors of <s>Hari</s>, <s>Varuṇa</s>, <s>Śakra</s>, <s>Hutavaha</s>, <s>Pitṛpati</s>, and the <s>Maruts</s>.
For a Brahmin it should be white like a conch, a white water-lily, or crystal; for a Kṣatriya it should resemble the eye of a brown hare.
For a Vaiśya it should be like a bright plantain leaf; for a Śūdra it should have the brilliance of a polished sword.

children.text: dvau vajravarṇau pṛthivīpatīnāṃ sadbhiḥ pradiṣṭau na tu sārvajanyau
children.translated_text: Two diamond colors have been prescribed by the good for kings, but they are not for everyone:
one that is red like hibiscus or broken coral, or one that resembles the juice of turmeric.
Because he is lord over all varṇas, a king may wear one suitable to any varṇa if it is endowed with qualities,
according to his wish; but no one else may ever wear what belongs to another.
Just as a mixture of varṇas may occur through lower and higher modes of conduct,
so a mixture among the colors of diamonds is considered still more troublesome.

children.text: na ca mārgavibhāgamātravṛttyā viduṣā vajraparigraho vidheyaḥ
children.translated_text: A wise person should not acquire a diamond merely by following the conventional division of classes.
A diamond possessed of qualities is the prosperity of those endowed with qualities; the opposite is the cause of the rise of calamity.

children.text: ekamapi yasya śṛṅgaṃ vidalitamavalokyate viśīrṇaṃ vā
children.translated_text: Even if it has good qualities, a diamond whose single point is seen to be split or broken
should not be worn in the house by those who seek good fortune.
A diamond with its point-region cracked, burnt, or broken, and with its middle covered by spots of bad color,

children.text: na hi vajrabhṛto 'pi vajramāśu śriyamapyāśrayalālasāṃ na kuryāt ||
children.translated_text: will not quickly make even fortune, though eager for an abode, come to the bearer of the diamond.
If one part of it has the appearance of blood, or if it is variegated with red color,
then, when worn, it will quickly bring shame, and even the end of life by sudden death.
Edges, sides, and lower cutting-lines are said to be six, eight, and twelve;
lofty, even, and sharp-pointed forms are the mine-born qualities of diamond.

children.text: ṣaṭkoṭi śuddham amalaṃ sphuṭatīkṣṇadhāraṃ varṇānvitaṃ laghu supārśvam apetadoṣam
children.translated_text: A six-edged diamond that is pure, stainless, clear, sharp-edged, endowed with color, light, well-sided, and free from defects...

children.text: indrāyudhāṃśuvisṛtichuritāntarikṣam evaṃvidhaṃ bhuvi bhavetsulabhaṃ na vajram ||
children.translated_text: A diamond of such a kind, with the sky about it tinged by the streaming rays of <s>Indra</s>'s bow, is not easily found on earth.

children.text: tīkṣṇāgraṃ vimalamapetasarvadoṣaṃ dhatte yaḥ prayatatanuḥ sadaiva vajram
children.translated_text: A man of purified body who always wears a diamond that has a sharp point, is clear, and is free from every fault,
has increase come to him day by day as long as he lives: women, prosperity, sons, wealth, grain, cattle, and horses.
Dangers from serpents, fire, poison, tigers, thieves, and water,
and also rites of the <s>Atharvaṇa</s> kind, turn back from him from afar.
If one should wear a diamond free of every defect, twenty rice-grains in weight,
those who know the jewel-science say that its highest price is two lakhs of rūpakas.
Less by a third, then a half, then with half of that remaining, a thirteenth, then thirty and half-portions thereafter,
an eightieth part, then a hundredth part, and a thousandth part: this is the reckoning with the smaller equal reductions.

children.text: yattaṇḍulairdvādaśabhiḥ kṛtasya vajrasya mūlyaṃ prathamaṃ pradiṣṭam
children.translated_text: The value first prescribed for a diamond made up to twelve rice-grains
is thus the fixed determination for one that has successively come down by two, or for one deficient by a single measure.
Nor indeed is the scale for weighing diamonds made by rice-grains alone.
One should reckon a rice-grain by eight pale mustard seeds.
But a diamond that is endowed with all qualities and floats in water
is approved for wearing above the whole class of jewels.
When a diamond is spoiled even by a small fault, visible or invisible,

children.text: svamūlyād daśamaṃ bhāgaṃ vajraṃ labhati mānavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: a man obtains only a tenth part of its proper value.
For a diamond showing many manifest faults, whether small or large,
even a hundredth part of its proper value is not prescribed.
If a diamond with a clear fault is nevertheless seen in an ornament,
its value should be slight, fit only for the working of other jewels.

children.text: prathamaṃ guṇasampadābhyupetaṃ pratibaddhaṃ samupaiti yacca doṣam
children.translated_text: A diamond that was first furnished with excellence, but acquires a fault once it has been set,

children.text: alamābharaṇena tasya rājño guṇahīno 'pi maṇirna bhūṣaṇāya ||
children.translated_text: is enough as an ornament for that king; a jewel without qualities is not an adornment.
A woman who desires to bear sons should not wear a diamond, even if it has good qualities,
except one that is free from bad traits such as being long, flattened, or triangular.
With iron, topaz, and likewise gomedaka,
with cat's-eye and crystal, and also with different kinds of glass,
skilled people make imitations of diamond.
Among these, examination must be made by learned and excellent testers.
Their testing should be done by alkali, scraping, and touchstones.

children.text: pṛthivyāṃ yāni ratnāni ye cānye lohadhātavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: All the jewels on earth, and whatever other metallic ores there are,
a diamond scratches them all, and it is not scratched by them.
For all jewels, heaviness is the cause and basis of high value.
In the case of a diamond, wise men declare the reverse of that.
A genuine one scratches a non-genuine one; kuruvinda diamonds scratch a genuine one.
By diamonds one scratches diamond; diamond is not scratched by anything else.

children.text: vajrāṇi muktāmaṇayo ye ca kecana jātayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Diamonds, pearls, and whatever kinds of jewels there are,
when they are set, their radiance does not go upward.

children.text: tiryak kṣatatvāt keṣāṃcit kathaṃcid yadi jāyate
children.translated_text: If, for some of them, because they have been cut crosswise, it somehow arises,
when they are being scratched sideways, that radiance is checked at the sides.
Even if its corners are broken, or it is marked with dots and lines, or discolored,
a rainbow-hued diamond still brings wealth, grain, and sons.
A king who wears, as prescribed, a diamond lovely with flashes of lightning
enjoys the land of all his feudatories, his enemies' might overwhelmed by his valor.

children.text: iti śrīgāruḍe mahāpurāṇe pūrvakhaṇḍe prathamāṃśākhye ācārakāṇḍe ratnatadviśeṣavajraparīkṣaṇādivarṇanaṃ nāmāṣṭaṣaṣṭitamo 'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the glorious <s>Gāruḍa Mahāpurāṇa</s>, in the first part of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa, in the Ācārakāṇḍa, the sixty-eighth chapter, named “Description of Jewels, Their Varieties, the Testing of Diamonds, and So On.”
<s>Sūta</s> said:
Pearls are famed in the world as arising from lordly elephants, clouds, boars, conches, fish, serpents, oyster-shells, and bamboo;

children.text: muktāphalāni prathitāni loke teṣāṃ ca śuktyudbhavameva bhūri ||
children.translated_text: and among them, those born from oyster-shells are abundant.

children.text: tatraiva caikasya hi mūlamātraṃ niviśyate ratnapadasya jātu
children.translated_text: Among these, only one ever properly enters the basic class denoted by the word “jewel”;

children.text: vedhyaṃ tu śuktyudbhavameva teṣāṃ śeṣāṇyavedhyāni vadanti tajjñāḥ ||
children.translated_text: of them, the oyster-born alone is pierceable, while those who know say that the rest are not pierceable.
Those produced from bamboo-pith, lordly serpents, and whales, and those born from conches and from boars,

children.text: prāyo vimuktāni bhavanti bhāsā śastāni māṅgalyatayā tathāpi ||
children.translated_text: are generally without full brilliance, yet they are commended because they are auspicious.
Of the eight kinds of pearls here proclaimed by those who know the ascertainment of jewels,
the conch-born is declared the lowest among them, and so is that which arises from the frontal globe of a lordly elephant.
A conch-born pearl has a color like the hue of its own source and is the size of a large lola fruit.
The one produced from within an elephant's frontal globe is yellowish and lacking in radiance.
Those conches that belong to the lineage of the excellent conch touched and drunk by the mouth of <s>Śārṅga</s>,
and elephants that are of pure lineage, are declared to be sources of pearls.
In these a pearl is produced round, yellowish in color, and lacking in radiance.
From a fish comes one that is the same color as the back of a pāṭhīna fish, well rounded, light, and very fine.

children.text: utpadyate vāricarānaneṣu matsyāś caite madhyacarāḥ payodheḥ
children.translated_text: It is produced in the mouths of water-creatures; these fish move in the middle of the ocean.
The pearl arising from a boar's tusk is declared to have the same color as the sprout of that tusk.

children.text: kvacit kathaṃcit sa bhuvaḥ pradeśe prajāyate sūkararāḍviśiṣṭaḥ
children.translated_text: Somewhere, in some region of the earth, it is born, distinguished by the king of boars.
It is taught that the pearl arising from the hard joint of bamboo has the beauty of a color like hailstones.

children.text: te veṇavo divyajanopabhogye sthāne prarohanti na sārvajanye
children.translated_text: Those bamboos grow in places fit for the enjoyment of divine beings, not in common ground.
The serpent-born pearl is of pure and rounded form like a fish, and in shape it has exceedingly bright beauty of color.
Its radiance is like the color of a sword-edge, utterly washed, flawless, and gleaming.

children.text: prāpyātiratnāni mahāprabhāṇi rājyaṃ śriyaṃ vā mahatīṃ durāpām ||
children.translated_text: Those who obtain such excellent jewels of great brilliance gain a kingdom, or great prosperity that is hard to obtain.
Those who have done merit become endowed with splendor through the pearl born from a serpent's head.

children.text: jijñāsayā ratnadhanaṃ vidhijñaiḥ śubhe muhūrte prayataiḥ prayatnāt ||
children.translated_text: When men skilled in the rules, purified and intent, seek jewel-wealth at an auspicious moment,

children.text: rakṣāvidhānaṃ sumahadvidhāya harmyopariṣṭhaṃ kriyate yadā tat
children.translated_text: then, after making a very great rite of protection, it is placed upon the top of a palace.
At that time the sky is covered by fresh clouds, with deep sounds like great kettledrums and spaces flashing with streaks of lightning,
by heavy clouds that bend low and hang down, laden with water.

children.text: na taṃ bhujaṅgā na tu yātudhānā na vyādhayo nāpyupasargadoṣāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Serpents do not harm him, nor demons, nor diseases, nor faults arising from calamities,
the man in the middle of whose treasury there remains a pearl produced from a serpent's head.

children.text: nābhyeti meghaprabhavaṃ dharitrīṃ vipradgataṃ tadvibudhā haranti ||
children.translated_text: The pearl produced from a cloud does not come down to the earth; when it has fallen away, the gods carry it off.
Its orb, made visible in the sky, covers the quarters with the brilliance of its rays and bears the brightness of the sun.
It overpowers all the light produced by fire, the moon, the lunar mansions, and the stars.

children.text: divā yathā dīptiṅkaraṃ tathaiva tamo'vagāḍhāsvapi tanniśāsu
children.translated_text: Just as by day it makes radiance, so too on nights sunk in darkness it shines there.
The whole earth, with waters lovely through the brilliance of varied jewels and furnished with the ornament of the four oceans,

children.text: mūlyaṃ na vā syāditi niścayo me kṛtsnā mahī tasya muvarṇapūrṇā
children.translated_text: would not be a price for it: this is my conviction, even if the entire earth were filled with gold.
Even a lowly man sometimes obtains it through the ripening conjunction of some great auspicious act.

children.text: sāpatnyahīnāṃ sa mahīṃ samagrāṃ bhunakti tattiṣṭhati yāvadeva
children.translated_text: So long as it remains with him, he enjoys the whole earth without rivals.

children.text: na kevalaṃ tacchubhakṛnnṛpasya bhāgyaiḥ prajānāmapi tasya janma ||
children.translated_text: The birth of that auspicious thing is due not only to the fortunes of a king, but also to those of his subjects.
For a thousand yojanas all around it turns away every misfortune.
Like a garland of stars scattered from heaven, the row of teeth of that great being,

children.text: vicitravarṇeṣu viśuddhavarṇā payaḥsu patyuḥ payasāṃ papāta
children.translated_text: pure in color among many-colored things, fell into the waters of the lord of waters.
The seed of that excellent jewel of great quality had the radiance of clusters of rays from the full moon.
That seed found a place among pearl-oysters; those which had existed before were of other origins.
In whatever region of the ocean the beautiful seed of the pearl-jewel fell,
there, cast upon by the water of rain-clouds and lodged in an oyster, it attained the state of a pearl.
<s>Saiṃhalika</s>, <s>Pāralaukika</s>, <s>Saurāṣṭrika</s>, <s>Tāmraparṇa</s>, and <s>Pāraśava</s>,
and <s>Kauvera</s>, <s>Pāṇḍya</s>, <s>Hāṭaka</s>, and <s>Hemaka</s>: these are the eight pearl-mines.
A shell-born pearl, not of very inferior color and marked by measure, form, quality, and brilliance,
is produced in <s>Vardhana</s>, <s>Pārasīka</s>, <s>Pātāla</s>, <s>Lokāntara</s>, and <s>Siṃhala</s>.

children.text: cintyā na tasyākarajā viśeṣā rūpe pramāṇe ca yateta vidvān
children.translated_text: The differences arising from its mine need not be considered; the learned man should strive for beauty and size.

children.text: na ca vyavasthāsti guṇāguṇeṣu sarvatra sarvākṛtayo bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: There is no fixed rule among qualities and defects, for every shape occurs everywhere.
Of this oyster-bright pearl, when weighed against another,

children.text: mūlyaṃ sahasrāṇi tu rūpakāṇāṃ tribhiḥ śatairapyadhikāni pañca ||
children.translated_text: the price is five thousand rūpakas, increased by three hundred more.
If it is less than that by half a māṣaka, its price is lower by two fifths.

children.text: yanmāṣakāṃstrīnbibhṛyātsahasre dve tasya mūlyaṃ paramaṃ pradiṣṭam ||
children.translated_text: For one that weighs three māṣakas, the highest price is prescribed as two thousand.

children.text: ardhādhikau dvau vahato 'sya mūlyaṃ tribhiḥ śatairapyadhikaṃ sahasram
children.translated_text: For one bearing two and a half māṣakas, its price is one thousand increased by three hundred.
For one whose weight is reckoned as two māṣakas, the price is said to be eight hundred.

children.text: ardhādhikaṃ māṣakamunmitasya samaṃ ca viṃśatritayaṃ śatānām
children.translated_text: For one weighed at one and a half māṣakas, the amount is three twenties of hundreds.

children.text: guñjāśca ṣaḍ dhārayataḥ śate dve mūlyaṃ paraṃ tasya vadanti tajjñāḥ
children.translated_text: For one that weighs six guñjās, those who know declare its highest price to be two hundred.

children.text: adhyardham unmānakṛtaṃ śataṃ syānmūlyaṃ guṇaistasya samanvitasya ||
children.translated_text: If its measure is one and a half and it is endowed with qualities, its price should be one hundred.

children.text: yadi ṣoḍaśabhir bhaved anūnaṃ dharaṇaṃ tatpravadanti dārvikākhyam
children.translated_text: If a dharaṇa is not less than sixteen, they call that the variety named <s>Dārvika</s>.

children.text: adhikaṃ daśabhiḥ śataṃ ca mūlyaṃ samavāpnotyapi bāliśasya hastāt ||
children.translated_text: It obtains a price of one hundred increased by ten, even from the hand of a foolish man.
If a dharaṇa is not less than twice ten, those who know call that the <s>Bhavaka</s> variety.
It obtains its proper price of seventy-nine, provided it is not devoid of excellence in qualities.

children.text: triṃśatā dharaṇaṃ pūrṇaṃ śikyaṃ tasyeti kīrtyate
children.translated_text: A dharaṇa complete with thirty is called <s>Śikya</s>.
The highest price for that is determined to be forty.
If it comes to forty, that kind obtains a price of thirty.
If it comes to fifty, it is <s>Soma</s>; its price is twenty.
If it is sixty, it is <s>Nikaraśīrṣa</s>; its price is fourteen.
Eighty and ninety are both called <s>Kūpya</s>.
Their values are eleven and nine respectively.
Then, taking all of that and cooking it in a food-vessel with the addition of lemon juice,

children.text: ghṛṣṭaṃ tato mṛdutanūkṛtapiṇḍamūlaiḥ kuryādyatheṣṭamanu mauktikamāśu viddham ||
children.translated_text: and then grinding it with soft, thin root-fibers, one should at once make the pearl pierced as desired.

children.text: mṛlliptamatsyapuṭamadhyagataṃ tu kṛtvā paścātpacettanu tataśca biḍālapuṭyā
children.translated_text: Having placed it inside a fish coated with clay, one should afterwards cook it gently by the cat-puṭa method.

children.text: dugdhe tataḥ payasi taṃ vipacetsudhāyāṃ pakvaṃ tato 'pi payasā śucicikraṇena ||
children.translated_text: Then one should cook it in milk, then in milky water, and again, when cooked, with pure sour liquid.
Then, when purified by rubbing with a spotless cloth, the pearl becomes endowed with abundant excellent qualities and beauty.

children.text: vyāḍirjagāda jagatāṃ hi mahāprabhāvaḥ siddho vidagdhahitatatparayā dayāluḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Vyāḍi</s>, of great power among the worlds, accomplished, learned, intent on the welfare of the wise, and compassionate, spoke.
A pearl that is bright like white crystal and joined with hundreds of golden rays
should be placed in the middle of mercury as an ornament for the body.

children.text: evaṃ hi siṃhale deśe kurvanti kuśalā janāḥ
children.translated_text: Thus, in the land of <s>Siṃhala</s>, skilled people act
when, in some pearl, there is suspicion that it is artificial.
One should soak it for a night in warm water containing salt and oil,
or it should be rubbed with rice, wrapped in a dry cloth.
But that which does not undergo discoloration should be known as not artificial.
A pearl that is white, of proper size, smooth, heavy, clear, and very pure,
with abundant brilliance and well rounded, is remembered as possessing good qualities.
A pearl endowed with proper size, weight, and rays, white, well rounded, and evenly and finely pierced,
which brings delight even to one who is not buying it, is declared to be a pearl of good quality.

children.text: evaṃ samastena guṇodayena yanmauktikaṃ yogamupāgataṃ syāt
children.translated_text: Thus, when a pearl is joined with the full arising of all these qualities,

children.text: na tasya bhartāramanarthajāta eko 'pi kaścit samupaiti doṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: not even a single fault among the host of misfortunes comes upon its possessor.

children.text: iti śrīgāruḍe mahāpurāṇe pūrvakhaṇḍe prathamāṃśākhye ācārakāṇḍe muktāphalapramāṇādivarṇanaṃ nāma muktāphalaparīkṣā nāmaikonasaptatitamo 'dhyāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the venerable <s>Garuḍa Mahāpurāṇa</s>, in the first section of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa, in the Ācārakāṇḍa, the sixty-ninth chapter, called 'The Examination of Pearls,' named 'Description of the Measures and Other Features of Pearls,' is completed.
<s>Sūta</s> said:
<s>Divākara</s>, the Sun, took the excellent jewel-seed, the blood, of that greatly majestic great demon
and set out to move through the expanse of the sky, blue as a sword-blade.
Then, halfway along, he was forcibly blocked by the lord of <s>Laṅkā</s>, whose mind was swollen with pride in his valor,
the constant conqueror of the gods in battles, as though by <s>Svarbhānu</s> himself.
The Sun released it into that best of rivers, whose deep great pools were stirred by the charming rounded hips of <s>Siṃhala</s> women,
and whose two banks were lined with betel-nut trees.
From then onward that river, equal to the <s>Gaṅgā</s> in the arising of the fruit of merit,
became renowned by the name <s>Rāvaṇagaṅgā</s>.

children.text: tataḥ prabhṛtyeva ca śarvarīṣu kūlāni ratnairnicitāni tasyāḥ
children.translated_text: And from that time onward, at night, her banks, heaped with jewels,
shine within and without as if sharpened and kindled by hundreds of golden arrows.

children.text: tasyās taṭepūjjvacārurāgā bhavanti toyeṣu ca padmarāgāḥ
children.translated_text: On her banks there are stones with brilliant and lovely color, and in her waters there are <s>padmarāga</s> gems;
there are also excellent stones arising from <s>saugandhika</s>, from <s>kuruvinda</s>, and produced from crystal.
They have the beauty of colors like bandhūka flowers, guñjā berries, whole indragopa insects, hibiscus, flax-flowers, and blood;
some gleam with the color of pomegranate seeds, and others with the appearance of kiṃśuka flowers.
Having colors like khindura, lotus, blue lotus, saffron, and even lac-dye,

children.text: sāndre 'pi rāge prabhayā svayaiva bhānti svalakṣyāḥ sphuṭamadhyaśobhāḥ ||
children.translated_text: even when the red is dense, by their own radiance they shine, clearly showing a beautiful center.
Having obtained the piercing contact of the Sun's rays through a mass of beams extending far,
those born from crystal and endowed with qualities color all their sides.
Some have a fierce red appearance like red lotuses mixed with safflower-blue,
while others have the lustre of aruṣkara and kaṇṭakārī flowers, and still others shine like cinnabar.
Some have the appearance of the eyes of cakora birds, male cuckoos, and cranes,

children.text: anye punaḥ santi ca puṣpitānāṃ tulyatviṣā kokanadottamānām ||
children.translated_text: and yet others have a lustre equal to the finest blooming red lotuses.
Through their combinations of power, hardness, and weight, the gems arising from crystal are generally alike;
the gems arising from <s>saugandhika</s> have a lovely appearance like dark-blue and red lotuses.

children.text: kāmaṃ tu rāgaḥ kuruvindajeṣu sa naiva yādṛk sphaṭikodbhaveṣu
children.translated_text: In the stones born from <s>kuruvinda</s> the color may indeed be pleasing, yet it is not such as it is in those born from crystal;
even though they have potency, they are without rays and are internally dense, while all are inclined downward.
But those <s>kuruvinda</s> stones that are born in the <s>Rāvaṇagaṅgā</s>
bear the dense red color of <s>padmarāga</s> while having the radiance of crystal.
Others in the <s>Āndhra</s> country follow their color,
yet none of them attains even a small fraction of their value.
Likewise, in the region called <s>Tumburu</s>, stones similar in nature to those arising from crystal

children.text: sadharmāṇaḥ prajāyante svalpamūlyā hi te smṛtāḥ ||
children.translated_text: are produced; but they are remembered as being of little value.
Excellence of color, weight, smoothness, evenness, clarity,
radiance, and greatness constitute the collection of qualities in gems.
Those gems that are rough, pierced with cracks, smeared with impurity, bereft of radiance, harsh, and discolored

children.text: na te praśastā maṇayo bhavanti samānato jātiguṇaiḥ samastaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: are not praised, even if they otherwise possess all the qualities of their kind.

children.text: doṣopasṛṣṭaṃ maṇim aprabodhād bibharti yaḥ kaścana kaṃcideva
children.translated_text: If anyone, through ignorance, wears any gem at all that is affected by faults,
hosts of evils such as sorrow, anxiety, disease, death, and loss of wealth attach themselves to him.
Although the five imitative sorts may be rather attractive among the classes,
a learned man should carefully recognize them as alien varieties.
Those produced in <s>Kalaśapura</s>, those arising in the lands of <s>Siṃhala</s> and <s>Tumburu</s>, and the <s>Muktapāṇīya</s> stones,
as well as the <s>Śrīpūrṇaka</s> stones, are similar but alien varieties of <s>padmarāga</s> gems.
Because of an admixture resembling husk there is the designation <s>Kalaśa</s>; because of a coppery condition, the one arising from <s>Tumburu</s> is so called.
Likewise, from blackness comes the kind born in the land of <s>Siṃhala</s>; from the nature of the sky comes the one designated <s>Mukta</s>.
The <s>Śrīpūrṇaka</s> is so called because it is formed without brilliance; the distinction rests precisely on the marks of an alien variety.
A <s>padmarāga</s> (ruby) that takes on a coppery hue, whose center seems filled as though by the contact of husks,

children.text: snehapradigdhaḥ pratibhāti yaśca yo vā praghṛṣṭaḥ prajahāti dīptim
children.translated_text: and one that appears bright when smeared with oil, or that, when rubbed, abandons its brilliance,

children.text: ākrāntamūrdhā ca tathāṅgulibhyāṃ yaḥ kālikāṃ pārśvagatāṃ bibharti ||
children.translated_text: and one whose top is pressed down, and likewise one that bears a black mark along its side under the fingers,

children.text: samprāpya cotkṣipya yathānuvṛttiṃ bibharti yaḥ sarvaguṇānatīva
children.translated_text: but one which, when obtained and lifted up, keeps its proper conformity and possesses all qualities in the highest degree,

children.text: tulyapramāṇasya ca tulyajāteryo vā gurutvena bhavettu tulyaḥ
children.translated_text: and one which, being of equal measure and of equal kind, is also equal in weight,

children.text: prāpyāpi ratnākarajā svajātiṃ lakṣed gurutvena guṇena vidvān ||
children.translated_text: the learned man should recognize, even when it belongs to the same class born from the mine of jewels, by its weight and by its quality.
If there is uncertainty and it does not disappear, one should scrape it on the touchstone.
Even after scratching them against each other with one that has arisen from a good source,

children.text: vajraṃ vā kuruvindaṃ vā vimucyānena kenacit
